planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Samantha's cream-and-green variegated foliage colors up best in strong sun and tends to revert to plain green in shade, so give it the sunniest spot available.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun after the last frost, and let the trailing stems spill over a wall, container edge, or raised bed where the foliage can be appreciated up close. Samantha is a low, spreading lantana cultivar grown as much for its striking cream-and-yellow variegated foliage as for its clusters of golden-yellow flowers, which deepen slightly toward orange at the center as they age. The variegation gives it season-long visual interest even between flushes of bloom, making it a popular choice for hanging baskets, mixed containers, and sunny groundcover plantings where its trailing habit can spread and cascade freely. Like other lantana, it is highly drought- and heat-tolerant once established and attracts butterflies heavily through the growing season; where winters bring hard freezes it is best treated as an annual or overwintered indoors.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Lantana cultivar notes

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Furman's Red is among the most cold-hardy Salvia greggii selections, regularly surviving winters that damage or kill other autumn sage cultivars back to the ground.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and avoid overwatering, since this Texas native subshrub is highly susceptible to root rot in soggy or heavy clay conditions. Furman's Red is a superior autumn sage selection valued for its true, deep scarlet-red flowers and its exceptional cold hardiness, which allows it to survive winters in colder parts of its range that would set back other Salvia greggii cultivars. It blooms in continuous flushes from spring through hard frost, drawing hummingbirds throughout the growing season, and its compact, well-branched habit needs only an occasional hard cutback in late winter to stay dense and floriferous. Extremely drought-tolerant once established, it thrives on lean soil and minimal supplemental water, making it a low-maintenance choice for xeriscape and pollinator gardens across the Gulf South.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Salvia greggii cultivar trials

common_name: Wild Thing Salvia (Vigorous Hot-Pink Hybrid Sage)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Wild Thing grows larger and more vigorously than most Salvia greggii selections, so give it extra room to spread.

directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and give this vigorous hybrid room to grow into a substantial, well-branched mound over its first two seasons. Wild Thing is a Texas A&M introduction resulting from a cross between Salvia greggii and S. microphylla, combining the best traits of both parents into a larger, more heat-tolerant plant that produces an especially heavy, near-continuous display of vivid hot-pink, two-lipped flowers from spring through frost. Its larger stature and exceptional bloom production make it a standout hummingbird and butterfly plant for a sunny border or mixed shrub planting, and like its parent species it is highly drought-tolerant once established, thriving on lean soil with minimal supplemental water. Cut back hard in late winter to renew growth and keep the plant from becoming woody and sparse at the base.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Salvia greggii x microphylla cultivar trials

common_name: Disco Belle Hardy Hibiscus (Dwarf Large-Flowered Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before the last frost or set out container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Disco Belle stays much shorter than older hardy hibiscus types, keeping its enormous flowers close to eye level rather than atop tall stems.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, and keep the root zone consistently damp through the growing season, since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant that wilts quickly if allowed to dry out. Disco Belle was bred as a dwarf, compact hardy hibiscus series reaching only 18–24 inches tall, far shorter than older hardy hibiscus types that commonly reach 4–6 feet, while still producing the same dinner-plate-sized, 8–10 inch flowers in shades of red, pink, and white, often with a contrasting red eye. The compact habit makes it useful for smaller borders, mass plantings, and containers where larger hardy hibiscus would be out of scale, and it dies back to the ground each winter, re-emerging reliably in late spring. Cut the dead stems back to a few inches above the ground in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Luna Red Hibiscus (Compact Deep-Red Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before the last frost or set out container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Luna Red is part of the compact Luna series bred for garden and container use, staying well under half the height of older hardy hibiscus varieties.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and often through summer to keep this wetland-edge native from wilting in hot weather. Luna Red is a compact, well-branched hardy hibiscus cultivar bred for garden and large-container use, producing an abundance of enormous, deep red, 6–8 inch flowers over a sturdy 24–30 inch frame that resists the flopping common in taller hardy hibiscus. It flowers continuously from mid to late summer into fall, providing bold, tropical-looking color from an entirely cold-hardy perennial that dies back to the crown each winter and returns reliably each spring even after a hard freeze. Cut the dead stalks back to a few inches above ground in late winter, and note that new growth emerges late in spring, so avoid mistaking a dormant crown for a dead plant.
